newsitem.title: NORWAY: Statoil sees low sales for Interconnector gasline.
newsitem.headline: Statoil sees low sales for Interconnector gasline.

text.p: Den norske stats oljeselskap AS (Statoil) said on Thursday the planned Interconnector gas pipeline between Britain and Belgium looked unlikely to meet its export potential of about 15 billion cubic metres per year from October 1, 1998.

"Prices in the UK market are currently close to the European level," Statoil's Status Weekly newsletter quoted analyst Tor Martin Anfinnsen of the group's natural gas marketing and supply division as saying.
"British gas suppliers have limited financial incentive to export another 10 billion cubic metres per year, since such sales would probably help to boost UK prices even further," Anfinnsen said.

The state energy firm and Norsk Hydro A/S withdrew from the Interconnector project in December 1994 because their main condition was not met. Both companies wanted British and Norwegian authorities to settle a long-running dispute over the Frigg gas line, which runs between the two countries.

"Only Conoco and British Gas Trading have so far contracted to use the Bacton-Zeebrugge link for gas sold from the Elgin and Franklin fields respectively to Russo-German distributor Wingas," Status Weekly said.

"British Gas ia actively seeking more customers in continental Europe. France's Elf, which needs more gas for its domestic customers, is also likely to export about two billion cubic metres per year through the Interconnector."

Norway's gas sales agreements from the Statoil-operated Troll field came into force officially on October 1. The field will send 90 million cubic metres per day of gas at its peak to the Kollsnes terminal on the west coast and on through several thousand kilometres of underwater pipeline southwards.
The sales agreements make Norway one of the top five suppliers of gas to Europe along with Russia, Algeria, the Netherlands and Indonesia.
